pos: n. (a man in the line of Christ; also a mountain in Psalm 68)
etymology: Hebrew Salmon, spelled Salma by the Chronicler and Salmon by Matthew. The same name belongs to a hill mentioned once in the Psalter, which is a separate place and not the man.
biblical_def: The book of Ruth ends with a genealogy, and this man stands in the middle of it: “And Amminadab begat Nahshon, and Nahshon begat Salmon” (Ruth 4:20), and then, “And Salmon begat Boaz, and Boaz begat Obed” (Ruth 4:21). The line runs on to its destination: “And Obed begat Jesse, and Jesse begat David” (Ruth 4:22). Matthew takes up the same names and adds the detail Ruth had left unsaid: “And Salmon begat Booz of Rachab; and Booz begat Obed of Ruth; and Obed begat Jesse” (Matthew 1:5). Salmon's wife was Rahab — the harlot of Jericho who hid the spies and hung the scarlet line in her window. So the great-grandmother of David was a Canaanite prostitute, and her daughter-in-law was a Moabitess, and both stand in the ancestry of Christ by name. The Chronicler spells the same man Salma and calls him the father of Bethlehem. A hill of the same name appears once and is a different thing altogether: “When the Almighty scattered kings in it, it was white as snow in Salmon” (Psalm 68:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) treats Salmon as a proper name; in Scripture, the son of Nahshon and father of Boaz, and also a hill in Samaria.
webster_full: SALMON, n. In Scripture, the son of Nahshon, husband of Rahab, and father of Boaz.
GENEALOGY, n. An account or history of the descent of a person or family from an ancestor; enumeration of ancestors in the natural order of succession.
LINEAGE, n. Race; progeny; descendants in a line from a common progenitor.
HARLOT, n. A woman who prostitutes her body for hire; a prostitute.
GRAFT, v.t. To insert a scion of one tree into another; figuratively, to incorporate into a stock not one's own.
scriptures: Ruth 4:20
And Amminadab begat Nahshon, and Nahshon begat Salmon,
Ruth 4:21
And Salmon begat Boaz, and Boaz begat Obed,
Matthew 1:5
And Salmon begat Booz of Rachab; and Booz begat Obed of Ruth; and Obed begat Jesse;
Psalm 68:14
When the Almighty scattered kings in it, it was white as snow in Salmon.
corruption_summary: Genealogies are skipped as dead weight, and with them the argument they carry — that God grafted Gentile outsiders into the line of the Messiah by name and on purpose.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Matthew's genealogy is an argument, not a formality. Four women are named in it before Mary, and the selection is deliberate: Tamar, who played the harlot with her father-in-law; Rachab, the harlot of Jericho whom Salmon married; Ruth, a Moabitess out of a nation barred from the congregation; and her that had been the wife of Urias. The evangelist could have run the line through the fathers alone, as the Old Testament usually does. He names these four because the gospel he is introducing is for such people.

The doctrine is sovereign, unmerited grace, and the genealogy states it in a form no argument can soften. Rahab did nothing to qualify for the line of Christ; she was a Canaanite prostitute in a condemned city who believed a report about the God of Israel and hung a scarlet cord in her window, and Hebrews lists her among the faithful while James cites her works as the proof of that faith. Salmon married her. Their son fathered Obed by a Moabitess, and four generations later David was king. A church that treats the begats as filler has skipped the place where God spelled out whom He saves.

pos: n. (a son of Japheth and the nation from him; also the wife of Hosea)
etymology: Hebrew Gomer, from a root meaning to complete or come to an end. Two persons bear the name: the eldest son of Japheth, father of a northern people, and the woman Hosea was commanded to marry.
biblical_def: The first Gomer heads a branch of the table of nations: “The sons of Japheth; Gomer, and Magog, and Madai, and Javan, and Tubal, and Meshech, and Tiras” (Genesis 10:2), with his own sons following: “And the sons of Gomer; Ashkenaz, and Riphath, and Togarmah” (Genesis 10:3). Ezekiel names the nation among the confederacy of Gog: “Gomer, and all his bands; the house of Togarmah of the north quarters, and all his bands: and many people with thee” (Ezekiel 38:6). The second Gomer is the hardest assignment God ever gave a prophet. Hosea was told to take a wife of whoredoms, and the record of his obedience is one line long: “So he went and took Gomer the daughter of Diblaim; which conceived, and bare him a son” (Hosea 1:3). She bore him three children with names that are sentences of judgment — Jezreel, Loruhamah, Loammi — and she left him, and God commanded him to buy her back. The marriage was a sermon Israel could watch. What Hosea did for Gomer is what the LORD did for a nation that had gone after other lovers, and the prophet paid fifteen pieces of silver and a homer and a half of barley to get his own wife out of another man's hands.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) treats Gomer as a proper name; in Scripture, the eldest son of Japheth, and the name of the wife of the prophet Hosea.
webster_full: GOMER, n. The eldest son of Japheth, the reputed father of the Cimmerians or northern nations.
JAPHETH, n. One of the three sons of Noah, from whom the nations of Europe and northern Asia are descended.
WHOREDOM, n. In Scripture, idolatry; the desertion of the worship of the true God for the worship of idols.
REDEEM, v.t. To purchase back; to ransom; to liberate or rescue from captivity or bondage by paying a price.
PROPHET, n. One who speaks by divine inspiration, or by the direction of God.
scriptures: Genesis 10:2
The sons of Japheth; Gomer, and Magog, and Madai, and Javan, and Tubal, and Meshech, and Tiras.
Genesis 10:3
And the sons of Gomer; Ashkenaz, and Riphath, and Togarmah.
Ezekiel 38:6
Gomer, and all his bands; the house of Togarmah of the north quarters, and all his bands: and many people with thee.
Hosea 1:3
So he went and took Gomer the daughter of Diblaim; which conceived, and bare him a son.
corruption_summary: Hosea's marriage is reduced to allegory or literary device to spare the reader its offence, which removes the very thing that made it preach.
corruption_paragraphs: Interpreters uncomfortable with a prophet commanded to marry a woman of whoredoms have long argued that Hosea 1 is a vision, a parable, or a later allegory. The text gives no signal of any of that. It names the woman, names her father, records three births with the dates of a reign attached, and follows the marriage through desertion and purchase. The dictionary takes the narrative as history because the book presents it as history, and because the power of the sign depends entirely on its being real. A parable about a betrayed husband costs nothing. Hosea's obedience cost him his household.

The point of the sign is the doctrine of covenant love that persists against unfaithfulness. Israel is the wife who went after her lovers; the LORD is the husband who says, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak comfortably unto her. Hosea does not merely forgive Gomer; he buys her, at a price, out of the position she had sold herself into. That is redemption in its plainest domestic form, and it is why the New Testament can speak of Christ loving the church and giving Himself for it. The nation was watching a man pay silver for his own wife, and the prophet meant them to understand exactly what they were seeing.

pos: n. (the grandfather of Achan, of the tribe of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Zabdi, meaning my gift or endowment. He is named only in the account of Achan's sin, where the lot narrows household by household until it reaches him and then his grandson.
biblical_def: The name appears in the sentence that explains a military defeat: “But the children of Israel committed a trespass in the accursed thing: for Achan, the son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took of the accursed thing: and the anger of the LORD was kindled against the children of Israel” (Joshua 7:1). One man had taken spoil from Jericho, and the text says the children of Israel committed the trespass. The search that follows narrows by stages: “And he brought the family of Judah; and he took the family of the Zarhites: and he brought the family of the Zarhites man by man; and Zabdi was taken” (Joshua 7:17). Then the household: “And he brought his household man by man; and Achan, the son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, was taken” (Joshua 7:18). And the whole house is gathered for judgment: “And Joshua, and all Israel with him, took Achan the son of Zerah, and the silver, and the garment, and the wedge of gold, and his sons, and his daughters, and his oxen, and his asses, and his sheep, and his tent, and all that he had” (Joshua 7:24). Zabdi is in the story because the lot fell on him first, and his grandson was standing in his tent.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Zabdi; the name belongs to the grandfather of Achan, of the family of the Zarhites in Judah.
webster_full: ZABDI, n. The grandfather of Achan, of the family of Zerah in the tribe of Judah.
ACCURSED, a. Doomed to destruction or misery; separated from the use of man and devoted to destruction.
LOT, n. That which in human speech is called chance; the determination of Providence by casting or drawing.
TRESPASS, n. Any voluntary transgression of the moral law; any violation of a known rule of duty.
SOLIDARITY, n. The state of being jointly and severally answerable; community of responsibility.
scriptures: Joshua 7:1

But the children of Israel committed a trespass in the accursed thing: for Achan, the son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took of the accursed thing: and the anger of the LORD was kindled against the children of Israel.
Joshua 7:17
And he brought the family of Judah; and he took the family of the Zarhites: and he brought the family of the Zarhites man by man; and Zabdi was taken:
Joshua 7:18
And he brought his household man by man; and Achan, the son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, was taken.
Joshua 7:24

And Joshua, and all Israel with him, took Achan the son of Zerah, and the silver, and the garment, and the wedge of gold, and his sons, and his daughters, and his oxen, and his asses, and his sheep, and his tent, and all that he had: and they brought them unto the valley of Achor.
corruption_summary: The account is rejected as primitive collective punishment, which passes over what the chapter actually teaches about a covenant community and the way sin is uncovered within it.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern objection is that a whole family suffered for one man's theft, and it is not a frivolous objection. Scripture's answer is not that individual responsibility is unreal — Ezekiel insists at length that the soul that sinneth, it shall die, and Deuteronomy forbids putting fathers to death for children. What Joshua 7 asserts is that Israel was one body under covenant, that a devoted thing hidden in one tent defiled the camp, and that the narrative itself records the sons and daughters being brought out with the silver and the garment, which suggests a household that knew what was buried under the floor.

The chapter's enduring lesson is the slowness of the exposure. The lot came tribe by tribe, then family by family, then man by man, and Zabdi was taken before Achan was. Achan stood through every narrowing round with the chance to speak and did not, until the lot reached him, and then he confessed fully and accurately. Sin hidden in the camp is not merely a private matter with private consequences; it cost thirty-six men at Ai before anyone knew why. The New Testament reasons the same way about a congregation — a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump — and gives the church a procedure precisely so the narrowing need not be by lot.

pos: n. (the youngest son of Hiel, who died when Jericho's gates were set up; also a son of Hezron)
etymology: Hebrew Segub, meaning exalted or lifted up — a name whose meaning stands in bitter contrast to what is recorded of the better-known bearer.
biblical_def: Five hundred years after Joshua pronounced a curse, a man in Ahab's reign tested it: “In his days did Hiel the Bethelite build Jericho: he laid the foundation thereof in Abiram his firstborn, and set up the gates thereof in his youngest son Segub, according to the word of the LORD, which he spake by Joshua the son of Nun” (1 Kings 16:34). The curse is quoted in Joshua exactly as it fell: “And Joshua adjured them at that time, saying, Cursed be the man before the LORD, that riseth up and buildeth this city Jericho: he shall lay the foundation thereof in his firstborn, and in his youngest son shall he set up the gates of it” (Joshua 6:26). Hiel lost his eldest at the beginning of the work and his youngest at its completion, and the historian's comment is four words long: according to the word of the LORD. A second and unrelated Segub belongs to the genealogy of Judah: “And afterward Hezron went in to the daughter of Machir the father of Gilead, whom he married when he was threescore years old; and she bare him Segub” (1 Chronicles 2:21), and “And Segub begat Jair, who had three and twenty cities in the land of Gilead” (1 Chronicles 2:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Segub; the name belongs to the youngest son of Hiel the Bethelite, and to a son of Hezron in the line of Judah.
webster_full: SEGUB, n. The youngest son of Hiel the Bethelite, who died when the gates of Jericho were set up.
CURSE, n. Malediction; the expression of a wish of evil to another; imprecation of evil, judicially pronounced.
ADJURE, v.t. To charge, bind or command on oath, or under the penalty of a curse.
FOUNDATION, n. The basis or groundwork of anything; that upon which anything stands.
FULFIL, v.t. To accomplish; to perform; to complete; to answer in event what was foretold.
scriptures: 1 Kings 16:34

In his days did Hiel the Bethelite build Jericho: he laid the foundation thereof in Abiram his firstborn, and set up the gates thereof in his youngest son Segub, according to the word of the LORD, which he spake by Joshua the son of Nun.
Joshua 6:26

And Joshua adjured them at that time, saying, Cursed be the man before the LORD, that riseth up and buildeth this city Jericho: he shall lay the foundation thereof in his firstborn, and in his youngest son shall he set up the gates of it.
1 Chronicles 2:21
And afterward Hezron went in to the daughter of Machir the father of Gilead, whom he married when he was threescore years old; and she bare him Segub.
1 Chronicles 2:22
And Segub begat Jair, who had three and twenty cities in the land of Gilead.
corruption_summary: The fulfilment is explained away as a later editorial insertion or as coincidence, and the historian's own explanation of the deaths is set aside.
corruption_paragraphs: Historical-critical treatment of 1 Kings 16:34 usually proposes that the notice was composed after the fact to vindicate the curse, or that Hiel's sons died of ordinary causes and the editor supplied the connection. The dictionary rejects that reading. The narrator states the cause plainly — according to the word of the LORD, which he spake by Joshua the son of Nun — and the books of Kings are constructed throughout on exactly this principle, tracking prophecies to their fulfilments across centuries. To excise the connection is to remove the thread that holds the book together.

The word itself faces no postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the patience of God's word. Half a millennium separates Joshua's oath from Hiel's building project, and in that interval nothing happened; the curse looked like a dead letter, and a man in the most apostate reign in Israel's history decided to find out. Scripture's consistent testimony is that delay is not cancellation — the Lord is not slack concerning His promise, and the same patience that spared Hiel for years spared him no consequence at the end. A father laid a foundation and buried his firstborn, and finished the gates and buried his youngest, and the historian names the boy.

pos: n. (the father of Bezaleel, the craftsman of the tabernacle)
etymology: Hebrew Uri, meaning fiery or my light, from or, light. He is named only as a link — son of Hur, father of Bezaleel — in the passages where God calls a craftsman by name.
biblical_def: The first man in Scripture said to be filled with the Spirit of God is not a prophet or a king but a craftsman, and his father is named every time he is: “See, I have called by name Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah” (Exodus 31:2). The filling and its contents follow immediately: “And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship” (Exodus 31:3). Moses repeats the announcement to the congregation in the same words, so that the appointment is public: “And Moses said unto the children of Israel, See, the LORD hath called by name Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah” (Exodus 35:30). And when the work is finished, the record credits him by his father's name once more: “And Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, made all that the LORD commanded Moses” (Exodus 38:22). Uri himself does nothing in the narrative. He is the middle name in a line that God troubled to specify three times.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Uri; the name belongs to the son of Hur and father of Bezaleel, the chief workman of the tabernacle.
webster_full: URI, n. The son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, and father of Bezaleel the craftsman.
WORKMANSHIP, n. The skill of a workman; the art of working; the execution or manner of making anything.
CUNNING, a. In Scripture, skilful; well instructed; experienced in an art; as a cunning workman.
ARTIFICER, n. An artist; a mechanic or manufacturer; one whose occupation requires skill or knowledge.
CALL, v.t. To name; to designate; to summon or invite; to appoint or designate for an office.
scriptures: Exodus 31:2
See, I have called by name Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah:
Exodus 31:3
And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship,
Exodus 35:30
And Moses said unto the children of Israel, See, the LORD hath called by name Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah;
Exodus 38:22
And Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, made all that the LORD commanded Moses.
corruption_summary: Spiritual gifting is confined to preaching and prophecy, so that the first man Scripture says was filled with the Spirit — a metalworker and engraver — is treated as an exception rather than a pattern.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is startling and plain: the first person in the Bible described as filled with the Spirit of God is a craftsman, and the contents of that filling are named as wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and all manner of workmanship — cutting stones, working gold, carving timber. Much popular teaching treats skill in a trade as a natural endowment and reserves the language of the Spirit for the pulpit. Exodus 31 does not divide them. God called a man by name, filled him, and set him to make hooks and boards.

The second thing worth noting is how carefully the appointment is published. Moses tells the congregation, using the identical formula God used to him, and names the man's father and grandfather and tribe. There is no anonymity in this work and no self-appointment either. Bezaleel does not volunteer; he is called by name and then taught to teach others, for God gave him also the ability to instruct Aholiab. That is the biblical pattern for skilled service in the church: divinely given ability, publicly recognised, exercised under the pattern God laid down, and passed on.

pos: n. (head of a priestly house whose register could not be found)
etymology: Hebrew Qots, meaning a thorn. The house of Koz held the seventh priestly course under David; at the return from Babylon its descendants could not produce their genealogy and were put from the priesthood.
biblical_def: Among the returning exiles were men who claimed priestly descent and could not prove it: “And of the children of the priests: the children of Habaiah, the children of Koz, the children of Barzillai; which took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and was called after their name” (Ezra 2:61). The result was immediate and severe: “These sought their register among those that were reckoned by genealogy, but they were not found: therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood” (Ezra 2:62). Nehemiah records the identical ruling in his own list: “These sought their register among those that were reckoned by genealogy, but it was not found: therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood” (Nehemiah 7:64). Yet the name is not left under a cloud. When the wall was rebuilt, a grandson of Koz is found working on it and working twice: “And next unto them repaired Meremoth the son of Urijah, the son of Koz” (Nehemiah 3:4). He appears again a few verses on, repairing another piece from the door of the house of Eliashib to the end of it. Barred from the altar or not, the house of Koz was on the wall.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Koz; the name belongs to a priestly family of Judah, the seventh of the courses appointed by David.
webster_full: KOZ, n. The head of a priestly house; in Hebrew, a thorn.
REGISTER, n. A written account or entry of acts, judgments or proceedings; a book of record.
GENEALOGY, n. An account of the descent of a person or family from an ancestor; enumeration of ancestors in order.
POLLUTED, pp. Defiled; made unclean or impure; rendered unfit for sacred use.
COURSE, n. The order of succession in which the priests served at the temple, by divisions.
scriptures: Ezra 2:61

And of the children of the priests: the children of Habaiah, the children of Koz, the children of Barzillai; which took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and was called after their name:
Ezra 2:62
These sought their register among those that were reckoned by genealogy, but they were not found: therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood.
Nehemiah 7:64
These sought their register among those that were reckoned by genealogy, but it was not found: therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood.
Nehemiah 3:4

And next unto them repaired Meremoth the son of Urijah, the son of Koz. And next unto them repaired Meshullam the son of Berechiah, the son of Meshezabeel. And next unto them repaired Zadok the son of Baana.
corruption_summary: The exclusion is read as bureaucratic cruelty, and the positive lesson — that a man barred from one office found another and laboured in it — is never drawn.
corruption_paragraphs: The ruling looks harsh to modern eyes: men who believed themselves priests were put out because a document was missing. But the priesthood was hereditary by divine appointment, not by conviction or self-assessment, and a man who could not show his descent could not stand between Israel and God on the assumption that he probably qualified. Ezra's governor added a mercy the objection usually omits: they were not to eat of the most holy things until there stood up a priest with Urim and with Thummim — the case was suspended, not closed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle worth recovering is what the house of Koz did next. Barred from the altar, Meremoth the son of Urijah the son of Koz shows up in Nehemiah's wall-building register repairing one section, and then a second section. He is one of very few men in that chapter credited with two pieces of work. A family excluded from the office it wanted did not withdraw; it picked up trowels. The New Testament's answer to the whole anxiety is that in Christ every believer's register is secure, for He is the High Priest whose genealogy and whose office are both beyond question.

pos: n. (a son of Korah; also a Kohathite and a son of Jeconiah)
etymology: Hebrew Assir, meaning prisoner or captive. Three men bear it, and the first is the most significant — a son of the Korah who was swallowed alive in the wilderness.
biblical_def: After the earth opened and swallowed Korah, a single verse in Exodus records what did not happen: “And the sons of Korah; Assir, and Elkanah, and Abiasaph: these are the families of the Korhites” (Exodus 6:24). Numbers states it outright — notwithstanding the children of Korah died not. The line continues through the Chronicler's Levitical register: “The sons of Kohath; Amminadab his son, Korah his son, Assir his son” (1 Chronicles 6:22). A third Assir belongs to the exiled royal house: “And the sons of Jeconiah; Assir, Salathiel his son” (1 Chronicles 3:17). What became of the first line is the remarkable thing. The descendants of a rebel who perished under the earth became the temple singers, and eleven psalms carry their name in the title: “To the chief Musician, Maschil, for the sons of Korah. As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God” (Psalm 42:1). The family of the man who wanted the priesthood by force ended up leading the congregation's worship by appointment.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Assir; the name signifies prisoner or captive, and belongs to a son of Korah and to two others.
webster_full: ASSIR, n. A son of Korah; in Hebrew, a prisoner or captive.
KORAH, n. A Levite who, with Dathan and Abiram, rebelled against Moses and Aaron and was swallowed by the earth.
LEVITE, n. One of the tribe or family of Levi; a descendant of Levi; one employed in the lower services of the temple.
PSALM, n. A sacred song or hymn; a composition designed to be sung in the worship of God.
MASCHIL, n. A title prefixed to certain psalms, signifying a didactic or instructive poem.
scriptures: Exodus 6:24
And the sons of Korah; Assir, and Elkanah, and Abiasaph: these are the families of the Korhites.
1 Chronicles 6:22
The sons of Kohath; Amminadab his son, Korah his son, Assir his son,
1 Chronicles 3:17
And the sons of Jeconiah; Assir, Salathiel his son,
Psalm 42:1

corruption_summary: Judgment is assumed to be indiscriminate and final for a whole family, and the plain record that Korah's children did not die — and later sang in the house of God — is overlooked.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the precision of divine judgment. Numbers 16 is cited as the great example of a family destroyed with its head, and the text says the opposite in as many words: notwithstanding the children of Korah died not. God's judgment fell exactly where He appointed it and stopped exactly where He appointed it to stop. Readers who use the chapter to argue that Scripture punishes indiscriminately have not read to the end of it.

The sequel is one of the strongest pictures of grace in the Old Testament. Korah's complaint was that the priesthood was reserved to Aaron; he seized a censer and was consumed. His sons lived, and their descendants were appointed by David over the service of song, and eleven psalms in the Psalter bear the heading for the sons of Korah. The men whose ancestor grasped at holy office by force stood in the house of God for generations, singing that a day in His courts is better than a thousand, and that they would rather be doorkeepers in the house of their God than dwell in the tents of wickedness. That is not a coincidence of the record. It is the point of it.

pos: n. (the father of Rizpah, Saul's concubine; also a Horite chief)
etymology: Hebrew Ayyah, a hawk or kite — the bird of prey named in the food laws. The name is remembered because of a daughter who kept the birds of the air off her sons' bodies.
biblical_def: Rizpah enters the record as a political grievance: “And Saul had a concubine, whose name was Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah: and Ishbosheth said to Abner, Wherefore hast thou gone in unto my father's concubine?” (2 Samuel 3:7). She reappears when David hands seven of Saul's descendants to the Gibeonites: “But the king took the two sons of Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, whom she bare unto Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth; and the five sons of Michal the daughter of Saul” (2 Samuel 21:8). What she then did is one of the longest single acts of endurance in Scripture: “And Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth, and spread it for her upon the rock, from the beginning of harvest until water dropped upon them out of heaven, and suffered neither the birds of the air to rest on them by day, nor the beasts of the field by night” (2 Samuel 21:10). She sat on a rock from barley harvest until the rains — months — driving off carrion birds from the bodies of her two sons and five others. David heard of it, and it moved him to act: “And the bones of Saul and Jonathan his son buried they in the country of Benjamin in Zelah, in the sepulchre of Kish his father: and they performed all that the king commanded. And after that God was intreated for the land” (2 Samuel 21:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Aiah; the Hebrew signifies a hawk or kite, and the name belongs to the father of Rizpah and to a Horite chief.
webster_full: AIAH, n. The father of Rizpah, concubine of Saul; in Hebrew, a hawk or kite.
CONCUBINE, n. A woman who cohabits with a man without the authority of a legal marriage; in Scripture, a wife of secondary rank.
SACKCLOTH, n. Cloth of which sacks are made; coarse cloth worn in mourning, distress or humiliation.
VIGIL, n. Watch; devotion performed in the customary hours of rest or sleep; a keeping awake.
INTREAT, v.t. To ask earnestly; to beseech; to supplicate; to be prevailed upon by entreaty.
scriptures: 2 Samuel 3:7
And Saul had a concubine, whose name was Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah: and Ishbosheth said to Abner, Wherefore hast thou gone in unto my father's concubine?
2 Samuel 21:8

But the king took the two sons of Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, whom she bare unto Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth; and the five sons of Michal the daughter of Saul, whom she brought up for Adriel the son of Barzillai the Meholathite:
2 Samuel 21:10

And Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth, and spread it for her upon the rock, from the beginning of harvest until water dropped upon them out of heaven, and suffered neither the birds of the air to rest on them by day, nor the beasts of the field by night.
2 Samuel 21:14

And the bones of Saul and Jonathan his son buried they in the country of Benjamin in Zelah, in the sepulchre of Kish his father: and they performed all that the king commanded. And after that God was intreated for the land.
corruption_summary: The passage is used to indict God for the deaths, or Rizpah is sentimentalised into a symbol, and the covenant breach that caused the famine goes unmentioned.
corruption_paragraphs: The chapter is read as one of the ugliest in Scripture and is often cited as evidence of a savage God. The narrative gives a cause the complaint usually omits: a three-year famine, an enquiry of the LORD, and the answer that it was for Saul and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites. Israel had sworn an oath to the Gibeonites in Joshua's day and Saul had broken it, and the land lay under the consequences of a violated covenant. Scripture is not commending the reprisal as a model; it is recording how seriously God takes a sworn word, including one obtained under false pretences.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour Scripture pays to a grief that would not be hurried. Rizpah could not undo the executions and did not try. She spread sackcloth on a rock and stayed from the beginning of barley harvest until the rains came, keeping the hawks — the very bird her father was named for — off the bodies. She had no standing, no power, and no legal claim. What she had was constancy, and it reached the king, and the dead were buried, and after that God was intreated for the land. The Bible does not tell her story in order to solve it. It tells it because she was there.

pos: n. (an older name of Kirjath-jearim, where the ark rested twenty years)
etymology: Hebrew Baalah, mistress or possessor — a Canaanite name the town carried before Israel took the land. It is identified in Scripture with Kirjath-jearim, the city of forests.
biblical_def: The name appears in Joshua's survey of Judah's northern boundary, with its equivalent given at once: “And the border was drawn from the top of the hill unto the fountain of the water of Nephtoah, and went out to the cities of mount Ephron; and the border was drawn to Baalah, which is Kirjathjearim” (Joshua 15:9). The line runs on past it: “And the border compassed from Baalah westward unto mount Seir, and passed along unto the side of mount Jearim, which is Chesalon, on the north side, and went down to Bethshemesh, and passed on to Timnah” (Joshua 15:10). The town matters because of what was kept there. After the Philistines returned the ark, it stood in Kirjath-jearim for twenty years, and when David finally came for it the Chronicler used the old name: “And David went up, and all Israel, to Baalah, that is, to Kirjathjearim, which belonged to Judah, to bring up thence the ark of God the LORD, that dwelleth between the cherubims, whose name is called on it” (1 Chronicles 13:6). The parallel account calls the place Baale of Judah: “And David arose, and went with all the people that were with him from Baale of Judah, to bring up from thence the ark of God” (2 Samuel 6:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Baal as the chief male deity of the Phoenicians and Canaanites; Baalah is a town of Judah bearing the name, afterwards Kirjath-jearim.
webster_full: BAALAH, n. A city on the border of Judah, the same as Kirjath-jearim, the city of forests.
BAAL, n. The chief male deity of the Phoenician and Canaanitish nations; a lord, master or possessor.
ARK, n. The chest which contained the tables of the covenant, overlaid with gold and covered with the mercy seat.
BORDER, n. The outer edge or confine of a country or district; the boundary line.
CHERUBIM, n. plu. Celestial spirits; the figures of gold that overshadowed the mercy seat.

corruption_summary: The ark's twenty years in a private house are passed over as an administrative gap, and what that neglect says about Israel's worship goes unexamined.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what the long stay at Kirjath-jearim represented. The ark was the seat of God's appointed presence between the cherubims, and for twenty years it stood in the house of Abinadab on a hill in a border town with a Canaanite name, while Israel got on with other business. Samuel's verdict on the period is that all the house of Israel lamented after the LORD. The neglect was not a scheduling problem; it was a nation that had lost its centre and did not immediately notice.

The retrieval is equally instructive. David went to Baalah with thirty thousand men and a new cart, and Uzzah died reaching out to steady it, because the ark was to be carried by Levites on staves as the law required and not conveyed on Philistine equipment. David's own explanation three months later is exact: the LORD our God made a breach upon us, for that we sought him not after the due order. Zeal and gladness were genuine and were not enough. The same regulative instinct that governs the tabernacle's measurements governs the ark's transport, and Baalah is where Israel learned it again.

pos: n. (the eldest son of Ephraim, and head of the Shuthalhites)
etymology: Hebrew Shuthelach, of uncertain meaning. The name heads a family of Ephraim and recurs in a genealogy that hides one of the saddest short narratives in Chronicles.
biblical_def: The wilderness census lists him first among Ephraim's houses: “These are the sons of Ephraim after their families: of Shuthelah, the family of the Shuthalhites: of Becher, the family of the Bachrites: of Tahan, the family of the Tahanites” (Numbers 26:35), with his own line following: “And these are the sons of Shuthelah: of Eran, the family of the Eranites” (Numbers 26:36). The Chronicler repeats the descent: “And the sons of Ephraim; Shuthelah, and Bered his son, and Tahath his son, and Eladah his son, and Tahath his son” (1 Chronicles 7:20). And then, without warning, the register breaks into narrative: “And Zabad his son, and Shuthelah his son, and Ezer, and Elead, whom the men of Gath that were born in that land slew, because they came down to take away their cattle” (1 Chronicles 7:21). Two sons went raiding and were killed. The next verse is four words of grief inside a genealogy: “And Ephraim their father mourned many days, and his brethren came to comfort him” (1 Chronicles 7:22). Ephraim afterwards named another son Beriah, because it went evil with his house.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Shuthelah; the name belongs to the eldest son of Ephraim and to a descendant of the same house.
webster_full: SHUTHELAH, n. The eldest son of Ephraim, head of the family of the Shuthalhites.
EPHRAIM, n. The second son of Joseph, and the tribe descended from him, often standing for the northern kingdom.
MOURN, v.i. To grieve; to lament; to sorrow; to wear the customary habit of sorrow.
CENSUS, n. An enumeration of the inhabitants of a country; a numbering of the people by families.
COMFORT, v.t. To strengthen; to enliven; to invigorate; to console under calamity or distress.

corruption_summary: Genealogies are treated as lists with nothing human in them, and a father's grief embedded in one is read past without being noticed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture's registers are not inert. The line of Shuthelah runs son after son in the flat manner of every genealogy, and then a clause reports that two young men went down to take cattle from Gath and the men of Gath killed them, and the next verse says their father mourned many days and his brethren came to comfort him. A reader skimming for the next name will miss it entirely. It is one of the few places in a genealogy where a man weeps.

The detail also carries a quiet moral. The sons went down to take away their cattle — that is, they went raiding, and they were killed doing it. The Chronicler records the cause without comment and without excusing them, and then records the father's grief without qualifying it either. Both are true at once: the young men brought their end on themselves, and their father's sorrow was real and was worth setting down in the word of God. Scripture is consistently able to hold those two things together, and pastoral practice that must choose between them is poorer than the Bible.
